summary:
**Orbital Foundry** is an interactive multiplayer (1–4 player) space mission engineering and simulation game built in Roblox. Players physically move through a Vehicle Assembly Building, carry and stack spacecraft modules onto launch vehicles, configure missions at four specialized Mission Control consoles, launch their rocket, and pilot a deployed rover across planetary surfaces to scan science anomalies.

It addresses the challenge by turning abstract aerospace constraints into hands-on, interdependent trade-offs. Every hardware choice dynamically alters five live budgets: mass, power, cost, data downlink, and science yield. Working solo or collaborating across four roles (Flight Director, Propulsion Officer, Systems Engineer, and Payload Specialist), teams must balance competing priorities, test their spacecraft in live flight and surface operations, and review automated root-cause diagnostics after each mission.

Traditional STEM tools often isolate rocket design or orbital mechanics without showing how subsystems interact. Orbital Foundry provides an accessible, repeatable sandbox where students experience end-to-end systems engineering—learning through experimentation and teamwork how every decision shapes mission success.
details:
Orbital Foundry: Space Mission Architect is an interactive, multiplayer (1–4 player) space mission engineering and simulation game built on Roblox. Rather than treating rocket science as isolated math problems, it puts players inside a complete end-to-end aerospace workflow—from mission conception and physical spacecraft assembly to live rocket launch, planetary rover operations, and post-mission engineering diagnostics.

  • Asymmetric Mission Control & Role Selection: Players spawn inside a Vehicle Assembly Building (VAB) overlooking an outdoor launch pad. Up to four teammates claim specialized consoles—Flight Director (selects target orbit and authorizes launch), Propulsion Officer (chooses launch vehicles and manages mass limits), Systems Engineer (manages power margins, auxiliary batteries, and module stacking), and Payload Specialist (calibrates instruments and data downlink). In single-player sessions, a Solo Override automatically unlocks all consoles.
  • Physical Hardware Assembly: Players walk between illuminated hardware pedestals, pick up multi-part 3D spacecraft subsystems (solar arrays, S-band/Ka-band dishes, multispectral imagers, infrared spectrometers, synthetic aperture radars, and star trackers), physically carry them welded to their character through the VAB blast doors, and stack them onto the rocket on the Launch Pad.
  • Live Systems Engineering Trade-Offs: Every attached component dynamically recalculates five interdependent telemetry gauges on the Mission Control HUD: Budget ($M), Mass vs. Orbital Payload Capacity (kg), Net Power (W), Data Generation vs. Downlink Rate (Mbps), and Science Yield.
  • Launch & Playable Orbital/Surface Operations: When the Flight Director authorizes launch, main engines ignite with particle effects, cryogenic vapor, and camera shake as physics-driven ascent lifts the rocket into space. Rockets that meet orbital energy and mass limits deploy players onto a cratered lunar/orbital operations sector, where they pilot a six-wheeled rover carrying their exact assembled modules (WASD) and scan glowing science anomalies (E). Your engineering choices directly affect gameplay: net power determines rover top speed, star trackers sharpen steering response, and antenna downlink capacity multiplies transmitted science points.
  • Automated Engineering Review: After each mission, the simulation generates an efficiency score (0–100) alongside a root-cause diagnostic report explaining why subsystems succeeded or failed, allowing teams to immediately iterate and relaunch.

Benefits & Intended Impact

  • Bridges the Systems Engineering Gap: Traditional STEM resources teach orbital mechanics, power budgets, or rocket propulsion in isolation. Orbital Foundry demonstrates how optimizing one subsystem creates cascading constraints in others—teaching students how real mission teams balance competing priorities.
  • Transforms Failure into Active Learning: Overweight rockets stall on ascent, power deficits slow down surface rovers, and low-bandwidth antennas bottleneck science collection. By making consequences visible and immediately testable, students develop genuine engineering intuition through rapid trial and error.
  • Builds Collaborative Communication Skills: By separating authority across four distinct roles with shared budgets, teammates must negotiate trade-offs (e.g., whether to fund a heavier launch vehicle or downgrade a power-hungry radar) just like real aerospace engineers.
  • Accessible STEM Outreach: Built on Roblox, the experience requires zero specialized hardware or expensive simulation software, making university-level mission architecture concepts approachable for middle school, high school, and early undergraduate students worldwide.

Tools, Languages & Technologies Used

  • Game Engine & IDE: Roblox Studio & Roblox Player (cross-platform client-server architecture).
    • RemoteEvent architecture for real-time server-authoritative telemetry synchronization across all 4 clients.
    • RunService.Heartbeat & RenderStepped for smooth rocket ascent acceleration, rover driving dynamics, and launch camera shake.
    • WeldConstraint, VehicleSeat, and ProximityPrompt for physical object carrying, modular rocket stacking, and vehicle piloting.
    • Atmosphere, BloomEffect, SunRaysEffect, and dynamic Lighting transitions between sunset launchpad operations and deep-space starfields.

What Makes the Project Creative

  • Tactile Physicalization of Abstract Budgets: Instead of clicking menus in a spreadsheet, players physically haul solar wings and spectrometers across an assembly bay, watch their rocket grow taller stage by stage, and drive a rover whose physical speed and handling reflect their power and avionics math.
  • Connected Multi-Stage Gameplay Loop: Most space games end at liftoff or orbit insertion. Orbital Foundry links pre-launch engineering decisions directly to a playable post-launch surface exploration phase, proving why power generation, attitude control, and communications bandwidth matter after reaching space.
  • Self-Contained Procedural Architecture: The entire facility, telemetry HUD, dynamic progress bars, and diagnostic engine are generated cleanly from two modular scripts, making the simulation lightweight, reproducible, and easy to expand with new planets or instruments.

Key Factors Considered During Design

  • Balancing Realism with Accessibility: Real aerospace equations were distilled into five clear, interconnected metrics (Mass, Power, Budget, Data/Downlink, Science) with color-coded warning bars and plain-language diagnostic feedback so newcomers can grasp complex trade-offs within minutes.
  • Multiplayer Dynamics vs. Solo Playability: Role permissions were strictly enforced in 2–4 player sessions to encourage authentic teamwork and station switching, while automatically engaging a Solo Override mode when a single user plays alone.
  • Ergonomic Interaction & Visual Polish: Early testing revealed that standard line-of-sight checks could block interaction prompts while driving the rover over uneven terrain. We engineered custom range and line-of-sight overrides for smooth scanning, added neon floor pathways to guide player movement through the VAB, and included a toggleable Photo Mode (H) for clean presentations and demonstrations
